Clause References: ISO 26262-3 Cl.6 (ASIL A-D determined from severity, exposure and controllability); ISO 21448 Cl.6.5 (acceptance-criteria framework; quantitative values deferred to context); ISO/SAE 21434 Cl.15.8 (risk value 1-5 determined from impact and attack feasibility)
Consequence: Each framework addresses a distinct risk source (random hardware faults, functional insufficiencies, threat scenarios), and the frameworks are not interchangeable by design: they use different scales, input parameters and threshold definitions. The case study component receives ASIL D (ISO 26262), a project-specific residual risk threshold (ISO 21448), and a set of risk values per threat scenario (ISO/SAE 21434). No standard defines how to reconcile these into a single sufficiency judgement for the integrated top-level goal G1.

Clause References: ISO 26262-6 Cl.9 (software unit verification, MC/DC structural coverage at ASIL D); ISO 21448 Cl.9-11 (scenario-based testing, triggering conditions); ISO/PAS 8800 Cl.8-9 (AI metrics, uncertainty quantification); ISO/SAE 21434 Cl.10 (integration and verification, incl. penetration testing)
Consequence: The four evidence types are disjoint by design: each standard requires evidence addressing a distinct attribute of the system (code structure, scenario space, model confidence, attacker capability). They are produced differently (structural coverage analysis, simulation, ensemble inference, penetration testing), and each has its own measurement scale (coverage ratio, triggering condition coverage, AUROC, attack success rate). No standard prescribes how they combine into a single sufficiency claim at G5; the integrated V&V strategy is the engineer's responsibility. This evidence asymmetry is the WAISE paper's headline result.

Clause References: ISO 26262-1 Cl.1 (malfunction/fault scope, AI errors outside scope); ISO 21448 Cl.3 (functional insufficiency); ISO/IEC TR 5469 Cl.6.1 (systematic failure)
Consequence: The same AI behavioural error (e.g., missed detection) is: a systematic failure (TR 5469), a functional insufficiency (ISO 21448), and falls outside scope (ISO 26262, which addresses malfunctions only). This creates ambiguity about which assurance domain owns the error.

Clause References: ISO 26262-1 Cl.1.122 (confirmation of intended use); ISO 21448 Cl.3.37 (verification of SOTIF activities); ISO/PAS 8800 Cl.3 (AI validation definition)
Consequence: The term 'validation' has different definitions. A single V&V plan must clarify which definition applies at each point.

Description: Cybersecurity-SOTIF boundary not bridged at standards level
Clause References: ISO 21448 Cl.1 (explicitly excludes cybersecurity threats); ISO/SAE 21434 Cl.15 (includes threat scenarios such as adversarial perturbation); ISO/IEC TR 5469 Cl.8.5.1 NOTE 2 (security measures can conflict with safety)
Consequence: Adversarial point cloud perturbations cause false negatives: simultaneously a cybersecurity threat scenario (ISO/SAE 21434) and a triggering condition (ISO 21448). The G7/G8 boundary is not bridged at the standards level, leaving the allocation of evidence to either branch as a project decision.

Clause References: ISO 21448 Cl.13 (SOTIF field monitoring); ISO/SAE 21434 Cl.8 (continual cybersecurity activities, cybersecurity monitoring); ISO/PAS 8800 Cl.14 (AI operational monitoring, OOD detection)
Consequence: Three parallel monitoring scopes (AI, SOTIF, cybersecurity) operate on the same deployed component, and no standard defines their interaction. The same runtime anomaly (e.g., a sudden increase in missed detections) could be read as AI distributional shift, a new SOTIF triggering condition, or an adversarial attack.

Clause References: ISO/PAS 8800 Cl.8.4 (data quality requirements); ISO/IEC TR 5469 Cl.9.3.2 (data distributions linked to HARA)
Consequence: ISO/PAS 8800 Cl.8.4 prescribes data quality requirements but defers to context the threshold for when training data are sufficient. ISO/IEC TR 5469 links data distributions to HARA risks but without normative force.
